utterances.text: After we arrived at the train station, since I was someone who worked there, I contacted the stationmaster and asked him if a train was coming, and he said yes. And that large crowd of people kept waiting the train, which came at about half past eight, I think. It had ten carriages. There were some travellers but not very many. But in Ferizaj station, the train was crammed with people. In my view, there may have been around 2.500 people that boarded the train. The train set out in the direction of Elez Han, and we arrived in the train station of Elez Han.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember seeing police on board?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were policemen in the train.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you arrived in Elez Han, what happened?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: After we arrived in Han i Elezit, we stayed in the train up until 12.00. Since I used to know the stationmaster of Han i Elezit - his name was Davidovic - I asked him, "What is going to happen with us? Why are they letting us go further?" And he told me that, "We are trying. We are talking about the Macedonian authorities to let you in, but so far we have not yet received an answer from them." Apparently they were not willing to accept us. At about 12.00, this man, Davidovic, informed me that, "The Macedonian authorities do not want to take you in, so you have to go back." And this is what really happened. The train returned again to the Ferizaj station. We got off the train at this station in Ferizaj and we left the station and went each to our own house or wherever we could find shelter, and on the next day, we went back to the train station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the next train in the station full as the first one? Could you board on the next train?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: You mean on the next day?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, we could board on the train, but not all of us. A certain number of people managed to board the train, and we did, that is, get on the train, and went again in the direction of Han i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe how you crossed the border? How did you cross the border?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived at the train station in Han i Elezit, again I asked Davidovic, "What is going to happen to us today?" And he told me, because he already knew, that the authorities of Macedonia would accept us. And this is what happened. After five minutes of staying there, or ten minutes - I'm not sure - the train continued its journey to the border with Macedonia, which was not a normal thing to happen, because usually passenger trains shouldn't go up to the border but remain at the station. But in this case, the train went up to the border, and this happened also with our train. When they -- when the train arrived at the border, it stopped. Some Serb soldiers, with tractors and other vehicles, passed by on the road which ran parallel to the rails, and they told us to get off the train. When people saw police and soldiers, people were scared. At the moment I told them, "We should get off the train because this is what we are being told to do." And this is what we did. We got off the train, and for half an hour we were kept there, gathered at that place. After half an hour, they ordered us to walk in a line of two and get before the locomotive, in between the rails, and not try to leave the rails, because otherwise -- they told us that the ground is planted with mines. Therefore, we had to stay in between those two rails and walk along the rails. And this is what we did. We lined up by twos and walked up to the border with Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned soldiers and policemen. Did they wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the uniforms any different from the ones you pointed already, you indicated that you saw already?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No. They were the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Can I have the witness shown Exhibit 3, map 11, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, this is a map that will show a similar route to the one you described during all your testimony. The names are with the Serbian version. Can you please demonstrate or indicate to the Court how was the route that you took from your village, Staro Selo, or Fshati i Vjeter, up to the border?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This is my village, here where I'm pointing at now, at the crossroads of the roads Prishtina-Skopje and Ferizaj-Gjilan. I said that we arrived at the train station from the village, that is, in Ferizaj train station. On the day that we left Ferizaj, it was the 16th of April, for the second time. Then by train we walked -- I mean, we drove this way, up to the border, further than the usual train station of Han i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, Han i Elezit, when you say, is the same name as Djeneral Jankovic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same name. In Serbian it's Djeneral Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When did you return to Kosovo, Mr. Bucaliu?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: We returned to Kosova on 7 July of the same year, that is, 1999.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was your house in the same way as when you left?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No. It was burnt up, and the houses of my two brothers, who were living close by, as I said, were burnt, along with many other houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bucaliu, I wonder if you could just help us with the dates of some of these events. On the 14th of April, you left the village, and the next day you got to the railway station; is that right? The 15th, that would be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then you said a train was expected, and as I understand it, it arrived at about 8.30. Was that 8.30 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So would that be the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the 15th and on the 16th, because we boarded the trains twice. On the 15th, we went up to the border and came back. On the 16th, we did the same. Again we left in the morning, got off the train, and arrived at the border with Macedonia on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examined by Mr. Milosevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that until 1990 you lived together on good terms with the Serbs, that is to say, the Albanians and Serbs did, and that the situation was aggravated in 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The situation -- it's true, because until 1990, we were on very good terms with the Serbs, until that time. We used to invite each other to our weddings and funerals, with our Serbian neighbours, and then we would swap agricultural equipment and lend things to each other. But after 1990, these relations cooled, not with everybody, but with certain individuals, and they didn't behave in the same way as they had before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that you invited each other to funerals. Do people invite each other to funerals?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That is normal. When a neighbour dies, the village is informed and people are invited to the funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what do you say the reason is that your relations worsened in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The reason was, I think, quite simply, political, the politics pursued by the Serbian leadership. There were Serbian people in Kosova who supported this policy, and this is the reason why relations deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little while ago, you said that these were constitutional changes.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, the constitutional changes. Them, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when were these constitutional changes carried out?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The constitutional changes were in 1989.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why were relations worsened then in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I think the Serbs, at the beginning, perhaps were not great followers of Serbian politics, but slowly they too started to support them, and this was the start of this chill in relations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. This start of this chill of relations in 1990. And then why were there demonstrations, the well-known demonstrations of 1981? This was nine years before that.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: In 1979, 1980, 1981, I was at school in Slovenia, and I wasn't in Kosova at this time. But it is well-known to the public that Albanians were asking for their rights to be with -- equal with other republics in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in what were they not equal? In what way did they not have equal rights?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: They were not equal in the sense that it wasn't called a Republic of Kosova, it was called a Province of Kosova.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. But in Kosova, there are Serbs and Muslims and Croats and Romany. They all live there as well. Why are their rights not affected by that, only the rights of Albanians? Also the Gorani and Egyptians. That is to say, the rights of them all. There are several ethnic communities. Why were other rights, the rights of others not affected by this, only those of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: It's not true that the rights of others were not affected. The rights of others were affected just as the rights of the Albanians were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a special regulation pertaining to Albanians only and not pertaining to others or was there, on the other hand, regulations that pertained to others and not Albanians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Please, I am not involved in politics, and I am not able to give a proper consideration of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness's evidence was that relations worsened in 1990 or in the 1990s. Now, that's the matter on which he should be cross-examined. You've chosen to try and take events back, but as he tells you, he was at school at the time. Now, the 1990s may be of relevance to this trial. Earlier events, as far as this witness is concerned, in my judgement are not relevant. So ask him about the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I did not intend to ask him about that at all, but I was impressed by the fact that the Prosecutor referred to constitutional changes during the testimony of Mr. Bucaliu. Previously, he had spoken about his work as a railways man. So since this issue was raised, I raised it too. Also, since he claimed that until 1990 everything was fine, of course it is connected to that. It is only logical to ask why demonstrations were staged in 1981, which is before 1990. And also why there were demonstrations when the army intervened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't see the logic, but let us go on with what happened in 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let us go back to 1990 when, as the witness said, relations were worsened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1990, what kind of rights were taken away from the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I can only testify to the rights in the workplace where I worked. As I said before, we were deprived of the right to use the Albanian language as an official language in writing and in official communications in the workplace. This was one serious violation of our rights. And then such things were evident in other spheres too. I can tell the Court that on merely for one day's strike on which the Albanian workers were involved in, 130 workers were dismissed from the railways of Kosova and five of them were from Ferizaj. And the others who were not dismissed had their wages docked by 15 per cent for six months. Then between 1990 and 1999, not a single Albanian was taken on for employment in our organisation. Serbs were employed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll go back to this question, but the information I have here is that at your railway station, there were 28 employees out of which only six were Serbs. And you include one Romany in that figure. And all the rest were Albanians. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I said that the number of workers at the railway station fluctuated according to requirements. There were times when there were perhaps 28 and sometimes there were less. And sometime in the 1990s maybe it was like that but later on. But then other Serbs were employed at the station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in 1999, there were only six Serbs at the railway station out of a total of 28 employees. All the rest were Albanians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said in his evidence it was eight. Now, I don't think that much is going to turn on those two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am asking him about the actual figure, because he has given a descriptive explanation as to the Albanians being deprived of their rights, et cetera. I'm asking him about the figure because there are records about this. How many Albanians were there and how many Serbs were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: His evidence was 17 Albanians and eight Serbs. You're putting it was six and some others. It's not going to make a great deal of difference whether it was six or eight. So let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But even if he were right, do you bear in mind the fact that at any rate, even if your figures were correct, the Albanians were the majority in your enterprise, in your company?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what his evidence was, that as far as the railway station was concerned, that was the figures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. Let's go back to clarify this question of language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that until the regulations on the use of language were adopted, Albanian employees in the public company of railways wrote tickets in the Albanian language only, regardless of whether passengers were Serbs, Albanians, Turks, Muslims, whoever? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I said until 1990, the Albanian language was in official use in the workplace where I worked. And after 1990, we were deprived of that right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To put it quite precisely, according to law, the languages enjoyed equal rights and enjoy equal rights until the present day, but I'm talking about the actual implementation. Is it correct that until 1990, Albanian employees wrote only in the Albanian and that they would not even issue tickets in the Serbian language to Serbian passengers?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This would not have been a problem because until 1990, Albanian was an official language and tickets were written in Albanian until that time. But after 1990, this was punishable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was true that Albanian was the official language until 1990 and that it remained an official language after 1990, but the order that was given was that the Serb language had to be used as well, not only the Albanian language, and especially that Serb passengers had to be issued tickets in the Serb language as well. Why did that bother you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: It doesn't bother me at all. You should realise that Serbian passengers had tickets written in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that is the point. The forms for tickets, were they bilingual or monolingual?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember about the tickets, whether they were written in both, but documentation that we kept at the station was in Albanian, and the Serbs kept documentation in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what's strange about that? Why does that bother you, the fact that Serbs did not write in Albanian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you answer that? It may be it's not going to take us any further.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I can answer. We weren't bothered by the fact that the Serbs wrote in Serbian. It was not a problem. But we were bothered when we were deprived of the right to use Albanian, as we were allowed until 1990. We had no trouble until then at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no trouble because you did not use the Serb language at all; is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've taken this as far as we can go. He's given his answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, I would like to ask him kindly, because he does remember his work quite well, to answer the following question: The forms for tickets and the papers that he worked with at the railway station, were they in two languages or in one language? I claim that they were both in Serb and in Albanian, both languages, that is, and now you answer me: Am I right or not? Because there are documents there. It's not difficult to prove it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I said -- we're wandering around the same question. I said before, and I say again: Until the constitutional changes that took place in 1989, the Albanian and Serbian languages were used in the train station as official languages together without any problem, and after 1990, we were forced to write in Serbian, quite simply. We were not allowed to use our language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the answer is that the forms for tickets and the other papers were in two languages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until 1990, they were in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that, after 1990, they were no longer in two languages, these forms?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. After 1990, they were only in Serbian; only Serbian was in official use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. All right. And you assert that Albanian was not in official use in 1990?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his evidence about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know that according to the constitution, both the Albanian and the Serb languages enjoy equal rights, are equal in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I am not aware of the constitution in detail, but I know that in my workplace this right was denied us. So the Albanian language was not allowed in our workplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was Albanian not allowed or was it Albanian without Serbian that was not allowed?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it allowed to use the Albanian language simultaneously with the Serbian language when it was in use?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: After 1990, no, we were not allowed to use Albanian. That's a fact. I can prove it with books, with documents, with whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean documents like these?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I think we've dealt with this for long enough. The witness has given his evidence. We're going to adjourn now. Mr. Milosevic, we'll expect you to turn on to another topic tomorrow morning, not the language.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask him about whether he thinks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, would you be back, please, at half past 9.00 tomorrow morning to continue your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
